source.paper: Problem of the Week 2025-26 (from Volume 3, Set 10, Olympiad 4, 4B)

prompt:
When it is 7 AM in New York, it is noon in London. A plane leaves London at 12 PM (noon) London time and arrives in New York at 11 AM New York time the same day. A second plane leaves New York at 12 PM (noon) New York time for London.

**What time in London is it when the second plane arrives?** (Assume both planes fly for the same number of hours.)

solutions.title: Change everything to London time
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea.

- 7 AM in New York = 12 noon in London, so London is **5 hours ahead**.
- Plane 1 leaves at 12 noon London time and lands at 11 AM New York time = 4 PM London time. The flight takes **4 hours**.
- Plane 2 leaves at 12 noon New York time = 5 PM London time.
- 5 PM + 4 hours = **9 PM** London time.

**Answer: 9 PM**

solutions.title: Work in New York time
solutions.body:
- Plane 1 leaves at 12 noon London time = 7 AM New York time and lands at 11 AM New York time: a **4-hour** flight.
- Plane 2 leaves at 12 noon New York time and flies 4 hours, landing at 4 PM New York time.
- London is 5 hours ahead: 4 PM + 5 hours = **9 PM** London time.

**Answer: 9 PM**

source.paper: Problem of the Week 2025-26 (from Volume 1, Olympiad 46, #1)

prompt:
A purse contains 4 pennies, 2 nickels, 1 dime, and 1 quarter. Different values can be obtained by using one or more coins in the purse.

**How many different values can be obtained?**

solutions.title: Every amount up to the total works
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea.

- The largest amount is all the coins: $4 + 10 + 10 + 25 = 49$¢.
- Every amount from 1¢ to 49¢ can be made, so there are **49** different values.

**Answer: 49**

solutions.title: Build the amounts step by step
solutions.body:
- With the pennies alone: 1¢ to 4¢.
- Nickels and the dime make 5, 10, 15, 20¢. Add 0–4 pennies to each, and you get **every amount from 1¢ to 24¢**.
- Now add the quarter (25¢) to any of those (or use it alone): every amount from 25¢ to 49¢.
- So all amounts 1¢ through 49¢ are possible: 49 values.

**Answer: 49**

source.paper: Problem of the Week 2025-26 (from Volume 1, Olympiad 55, #3)

prompt:
Two students are needed to work in the school store during the lunch hour every day, and four students volunteer for this work.

**What is the greatest number of days that can be arranged in which no pair of the four students works together more than once?**

solutions.title: List all the pairs
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea.

Call the students A, B, C, D. The different pairs are:

AB, AC, AD, BC, BD, CD

That is 6 pairs (AB and BA are the same pair). Each day uses a new pair, so there can be **6** days.

**Answer: 6 days**

solutions.title: Count and divide by 2
solutions.body:
- Each student can be paired with 3 others: $4 \times 3 = 12$.
- Each pair was counted twice (once for each person), so there are $12 \div 2 = 6$ pairs, one per day.

**Answer: 6 days**

source.paper: Problem of the Week 2025-26 (from Volume 1, Olympiad 49, #2)

prompt:
Twenty-four meters of fencing is used to fence a rectangular garden. Let $M$ represent the number of square meters in the area of the garden.

**What is the largest value that $M$ could have?**

solutions.title: Make a table
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea.

The perimeter is 24 m, so length + width = **12 m** (half the perimeter).

| Length | Width | Area |
|---|---|---|
| 11 | 1 | 11 |
| 10 | 2 | 20 |
| 9 | 3 | 27 |
| 8 | 4 | 32 |
| 7 | 5 | 35 |
| 6 | 6 | **36** |

The largest area is 36 square meters.

**Answer: 36**

solutions.title: A square gives the most area
solutions.body:
- For a fixed perimeter, the closer the rectangle is to a square, the bigger its area.
- A square with perimeter 24 m has sides $24 \div 4 = 6$ m.
- Area $= 6 \times 6 = 36$ square meters.

**Answer: 36**

source.paper: Problem of the Week 2025-26 (from Volume 1, Olympiad 35, #4)

prompt:
Alice started a Math Club during the first week of school. As the only member, she decided to recruit two new members during the following week of school. Each new member, during the week following the week when he or she became a member, recruits two new members.

**How many members will the club have at the end of five weeks?**

solutions.title: The new members double each week
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea.

| Week | New members | Total |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 (Alice) | 1 |
| 2 | 2 | 3 |
| 3 | 4 | 7 |
| 4 | 8 | 15 |
| 5 | 16 | 31 |

$1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = 31$

**Answer: 31 members**

solutions.title: Spot the pattern in the totals
solutions.body:
- Only the members who joined last week recruit this week, and each brings 2 people, so the number of new members doubles: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16.
- The totals are 1, 3, 7, 15, … — each is one less than a power of 2 (2, 4, 8, 16, …).
- After week 5 the total is $32 - 1 = 31$.

**Answer: 31 members**

source.paper: Problem of the Week 2025-26 (from Volume 1, Olympiad 20, #4)

prompt:
A circular track is 1000 yards in circumference. Cyclists A, B, and C start at the same place and time, and race around the track at the following rates per minute: A at 700 yards, B at 800 yards, and C at 900 yards.

**What is the least number of minutes it must take for all three to be together again?**

solutions.title: Find when each is back at the start
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea.

- In 10 minutes, A rides 7,000 yards, B rides 8,000 yards, and C rides 9,000 yards.
- Each of those is a whole number of laps (7, 8 and 9 laps), so all three are back at the starting point together.
- (Check smaller times: in fewer minutes, A and B can't both be at the same spot — see the second method.)

**Answer: 10 minutes**

solutions.title: Use how fast they gain on each other
solutions.body:
- B gains $800 - 700 = 100$ yards per minute on A. To meet again, B must gain one full lap (1000 yards): that takes $1000 \div 100 = 10$ minutes.
- C gains 100 yards per minute on B, so C and B also first meet again after 10 minutes.
- So the first time all three are together is at **10 minutes**.

**Answer: 10 minutes**

source.paper: Problem of the Week 2025-26 (from Volume 1, Olympiad 40, #2)

prompt:
The figure is a "magic square" with missing entries. When complete, the sum of the four entries in each column, each row, and each diagonal is the same.

**Find the value of A and the value of B.**

solutions.title: Use the full diagonal first
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea.

- The diagonal from the top right to the bottom left is complete: $12 + 9 + 5 + 8 = 34$. So every line adds to **34**.
- Third column: $7 + 9 + 16 + ? = 34$, so the missing bottom entry is **2**.
- Bottom row: $8 + 11 + 2 + B = 34$, so $B = 13$.
- Other diagonal: $A + 4 + 16 + 13 = 34$, so $A + 33 = 34$ and $A = 1$.

**Answer: A = 1, B = 13**

solutions.title: Find A + B first, then test pairs
solutions.body:
- The full diagonal $12 + 9 + 5 + 8 = 34$ tells us every line adds to 34. (A $4 \times 4$ magic square normally uses the numbers 1–16, whose total 136 split over 4 rows is also 34.)
- The other diagonal: $A + 4 + 16 + B = 34$, so $A + B = 14$.
- Numbers not used yet: 1, 2, 3, 6, 10, 13, 14, 15. The only two of them that add to 14 are **1 and 13**.
- Which is which? Try $B = 1$: the bottom row $8 + 11 + ? + 1 = 34$ needs $? = 14$, but then column 3 is $7 + 9 + 16 + 14 = 46$ ✗. So $B = 13$ and $A = 1$ (and the bottom row's missing number is 2).

**Answer: A = 1, B = 13**

source.paper: Problem of the Week 2025-26 (from Volume 2, Set 12, Olympiad 3, 3D)

prompt:
In this diagram, each "path" spells the word OLYMPIAD correctly, going down one row at a time. From any letter, a path may continue to **any** letter in the next row.

**How many different paths exist in the diagram?**

solutions.title: Count paths letter by letter
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea. Multiply the number of choices at each step:

- O → L: 2 choices → 2 paths
- L → Y: 2 choices from each L → $2 \times 2 = 4$
- Y → M: 1 choice → 4
- M → P: 2 choices → $4 \times 2 = 8$
- P → I: 3 choices → $8 \times 3 = 24$
- I → A: 2 choices → $24 \times 2 = 48$
- A → D: 1 choice → 48

**Answer: 48 paths**

solutions.title: Multiply the letters in each row
solutions.body:
A path picks one letter from each row of the diagram:

| Row | O | L | Y | M | P | I | A | D |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Letters | 1 | 2 | 2 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 2 | 1 |

Number of paths $= 1 \times 2 \times 2 \times 1 \times 2 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1 = 48$.

**Answer: 48 paths**

source.paper: Problem of the Week 2025-26 (from Volume 2, Set 6, Olympiad 3, 3D)

prompt:
One light flashes every 2 minutes and another light flashes every 7 minutes. Both lights flash together at 1 PM.

**What is the first time after 3 PM that both lights flash together?**

solutions.title: Use multiples of 14
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea.

- Both lights flash together every LCM(2, 7) = **14** minutes.
- From 1:00 to 3:00 is 120 minutes. We need the first multiple of 14 that is bigger than 120.
- $14 \times 8 = 112$ (too small), $14 \times 9 = 126$.
- 126 minutes after 1:00 PM is 3:06 PM.

**Answer: 3:06 PM**

source.paper: Problem of the Week 2025-26 (from Volume 2, Set 5, Olympiad 5, 5B)

prompt:
In one complete day, a man binds 100 books and his helper binds one-fourth as many books. They take turns working complete days.

**How many days would it take them to bind 500 books?**

solutions.title: Group the days in pairs
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea.

- The helper binds $\frac{1}{4} \times 100 = 25$ books a day.
- Every 2 days (one day each) they bind $100 + 25 = 125$ books.
- $500 \div 125 = 4$ sets of 2 days $= 8$ days.

**Answer: 8 days**

source.paper: Problem of the Week 2025-26 (from Volume 2, Set 3, Olympiad 4, 4C)

prompt:
Kim was elected class president. She received 3 votes for every 2 that Amy got. No one else ran. However, if 8 people who voted for Kim had voted for Amy instead, Kim would have received only one vote for every two that Amy would have gotten.

**How many people voted?**

solutions.title: Think in equal groups
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea.

- At first, the voters split into 5 equal groups: 3 for Kim, 2 for Amy.
- After the switch, they split into 3 equal groups: 1 for Kim, 2 for Amy.
- So the number of voters is a multiple of both 5 and 3: 15, 30, 45, …
- Try 15: Kim 9, Amy 6. After 8 switch: Kim 1, Amy 14. Not 1 : 2. ✗
- Try 30: Kim 18, Amy 12. After 8 switch: Kim 10, Amy 20. That is 1 : 2 ✓

**Answer: 30 people**

solutions.title: Compare Kim's share
solutions.body:
- Before: Kim had $\frac{3}{5}$ of the votes. After: Kim has $\frac{1}{3}$ of the votes.
- The 8 switched votes are the difference: $\frac{3}{5} - \frac{1}{3} = \frac{9}{15} - \frac{5}{15} = \frac{4}{15}$ of all the votes.
- If $\frac{4}{15}$ of the votes is 8, then $\frac{1}{15}$ is 2, and all the votes are $15 \times 2 = 30$.

**Answer: 30 people**

source.paper: Problem of the Week 2025-26 (from Volume 3, Set 16, Olympiad 5, 5D)

prompt:
This year, 1 out of every 55 adults started a new business. This rate represented an increase of 20% over last year's rate of 1 new business start-up out of every $N$ adults.

**Find $N$.**

solutions.title: Use the meaning of percent
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea.

- Last year's rate was $\frac{1}{N}$; this year's is $\frac{1}{55}$.
- A 20% increase means this year's rate is 1.2 times last year's: $1.2 \times \frac{1}{N} = \frac{1}{55}$.
- So $\frac{1.2}{N} = \frac{1}{55}$, which means $N = 1.2 \times 55 = 66$.

**Answer: $N = 66$**

solutions.title: Think about a big group of adults
solutions.body:
- Picture 330 adults (a number that 55 and 66 both divide nicely).
- This year: 1 out of every 55 → $330 \div 55 = 6$ new businesses.
- 6 is a 20% increase over last year, so last year there were 5 (because $5 + 20\% \text{ of } 5 = 5 + 1 = 6$).
- Last year 5 out of 330 adults, which is 1 out of every $330 \div 5 = 66$.

**Answer: $N = 66$**

source.paper: Problem of the Week 2025-26 (from Volume 3, Set 13, Olympiad 2, 2E)

prompt:
Jess runs an outdoor stand at City Stadium. When it rains, Jess earns \$1500 selling umbrellas. But when it doesn't rain, she earns \$400 selling sunglasses. On any given day, the chance of rain is 40%.

**On the average, how much can Jess expect to earn daily?**

solutions.title: Imagine 100 days
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea.

- In 100 days, about 40 are rainy and 60 are dry.
- Earnings: $40 \times \$1500 + 60 \times \$400 = \$60{,}000 + \$24{,}000 = \$84{,}000$.
- Average per day: $\$84{,}000 \div 100 = \$840$.

**Answer: \$840**

solutions.title: Imagine 5 days
solutions.body:
40% is 2 out of 5.

- In 5 days: 2 rainy days and 3 dry days.
- Earnings: $2 \times \$1500 + 3 \times \$400 = \$3000 + \$1200 = \$4200$.
- Per day: $\$4200 \div 5 = \$840$.

**Answer: \$840**

source.paper: Problem of the Week 2025-26 (from Volume 3, Set 6, Olympiad 2, 2C)

prompt:
There are 2 red cars and 3 blue cars. The 5 cars contain a total of 12 people. No car has more than 4 people. Every car has at least 1 person. The only cars with the same number of people are the red cars.

**How many people are in 1 red car?**

solutions.title: Start with all different numbers
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea.

- If all 5 cars had different numbers of people, the smallest total would be $1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 15$.
- But there are only 12 people and no car may have 5. Take 3 people out of the "5" car: $1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 2 = 12$.
- The two cars with the same number (2) are the red cars.

**Answer: 2 people**

solutions.title: The blue cars plus one red car use 1, 2, 3, 4
solutions.body:
- The 3 blue cars and one red car all have **different** numbers from 1 to 4, so together they use exactly 1, 2, 3 and 4: that is $1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10$ people.
- The second red car holds the rest: $12 - 10 = 2$ people.
- Both red cars have the same number, so each red car has 2.

**Answer: 2 people**

source.paper: Problem of the Week 2025-26 (from Volume 3, Set 4, Olympiad 5, 5C)

prompt:
In the following, different letters represent different digits (see the picture: ONE + FOUR = FIVE and ONE × 4 = FOUR).

**What digit does the letter O represent?**

solutions.title: Use the addition and the multiplication
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea.

- O is a leading digit, so O ≠ 0.
- In ONE + FOUR = FIVE, the thousands digit F stays F, so nothing carries out of the hundreds column, where O + O is added. So O + O is less than 10: O is 1, 2, 3 or 4.
- In ONE × 4 = FOUR, the leftmost part $4 \times O$ (plus a carry of 0–3 from the tens) must make the two-digit number "FO", which ends in O:
  - O = 1: $4 + \text{carry}$ must end in 1 — impossible.
  - O = 2: $8 + \text{carry}$ must end in 2 — impossible.
  - O = 3: $12 + 1 = 13$ ends in 3 ✓ (F = 1)
  - O = 4: $16 + \text{carry}$ must end in 4 — impossible.

**Answer: 3**

solutions.title: Size up the multiplication
solutions.body:
- FOUR $= 4 \times$ ONE is a 4-digit number, so ONE is at least 250, and FOUR starts with F.
- ONE is less than 500 here (O ≤ 4 from the addition), so FOUR is less than 2000: **F = 1**.
- Then FOUR is in the 1000s with hundreds digit O, so it is between $1000 + 100 \times O$ and $1099 + 100 \times O$. Dividing by 4, ONE is about $250 + 25 \times O$ to $275 + 25 \times O$.
- ONE must start with O:
  - O = 1: ONE would be 275–299, which starts with 2 ✗
  - O = 2: ONE would be 300–324, which starts with 3 ✗
  - O = 3: ONE would be 325–349, which starts with 3 ✓
  - O = 4: ONE would be 350–374, which starts with 3 ✗

**Answer: 3**

source.paper: Problem of the Week 2025-26 (from Volume 3, Set 15, Olympiad 1, 1B)

prompt:
In a hotel, 40 people occupy exactly 26 rooms. Each room is occupied by either one or two people.

**How many rooms are occupied by exactly one person?**

solutions.title: Start with 1 person per room
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea.

- Put 1 person in each of the 26 rooms. That uses 26 people, leaving $40 - 26 = 14$.
- Put those 14 extra people into 14 different rooms, so 14 rooms have 2 people.
- The other $26 - 14 = 12$ rooms have exactly one person.

**Answer: 12 rooms**

solutions.title: Start with 2 people per room
solutions.body:
- If all 26 rooms had 2 people, there would be 52 people.
- That's $52 - 40 = 12$ too many. Each room with only 1 person removes 1 from the count.
- So 12 rooms have exactly one person. (Check: $12 \times 1 + 14 \times 2 = 12 + 28 = 40$ ✓)

**Answer: 12 rooms**

source.paper: Problem of the Week 2025-26 (from Volume 3, Set 10, Olympiad 5, 5D)

prompt:
A square with an area of 18 square centimeters is inscribed in a circle as shown.

**Using the approximation $\pi \approx 3.14$, find the area of the shaded region to the nearest square centimeter.**

solutions.title: Draw the diagonals
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea.

- Shaded area = circle area − square area.
- Draw both diagonals of the square. They cut it into 4 equal right triangles, each with area $18 \div 4 = 4.5$.
- The diagonals are diameters of the circle, so each triangle has two legs equal to the radius $r$: $\frac{1}{2} \times r \times r = 4.5$, so $r \times r = 9$ and $r = 3$ cm.
- Circle area $\approx 3.14 \times 3 \times 3 = 28.26$.
- Shaded area $\approx 28.26 - 18 = 10.26$, which rounds to **10**.

**Answer: 10 sq cm**

solutions.title: Compare with the big square around the circle
solutions.body:
- Draw a big square around the circle, touching it. Its side is the diameter.
- The small square (corners on the circle) has exactly **half** the area of the big square (fold the big square's corners in and they cover the small square). So the big square has area $2 \times 18 = 36$, its side is 6, and the radius is 3.
- Circle area $\approx 3.14 \times 9 = 28.26$.
- Shaded $\approx 28.26 - 18 = 10.26 \approx 10$.

**Answer: 10 sq cm**

source.paper: Problem of the Week 2025-26 (from Volume 3, Set 7, Olympiad 2, 2B)

prompt:
In the repeating pattern below, what will be the 78th letter written?

ABBCCD ABBCCD … (and so on)

solutions.title: Find the length of the repeating part
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea.

- The block ABBCCD has 6 letters and then repeats.
- $78 \div 6 = 13$ exactly, so the first 78 letters are 13 complete blocks.
- The 78th letter is the last letter of a block, which is **D**.

**Answer: D**

solutions.title: Use a nearby multiple
solutions.body:
- Letters 6, 12, 18, … (multiples of 6) are always D.
- 78 is $6 \times 13$, a multiple of 6, so letter 78 is D.
- Check: letter 72 is D, then 73 A, 74 B, 75 B, 76 C, 77 C, **78 D**.

**Answer: D**

source.paper: Problem of the Week 2025-26 (from Volume 3, Set 4, Olympiad 1, 1D)

prompt:
Janine's number has three digits. One digit is a prime number. Another digit is a square number. The other digit is neither prime nor square. Her number is NOT divisible by 3.

**What is the greatest possible value of Janine's number?**

solutions.title: Sort the digits into groups
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea.

- Prime digits: 2, 3, 5, 7.
- Square digits: 0, 1, 4, 9.
- Neither: 6, 8.
- Take the biggest from each group and arrange from largest to smallest: 987. But $9 + 8 + 7 = 24$, which is divisible by 3, so 987 is divisible by 3. ✗
- Use the next biggest prime, 5: **985**. $9 + 8 + 5 = 22$, not divisible by 3 ✓

**Answer: 985**

solutions.title: Count down from the top
solutions.body:
Look at the biggest numbers starting with 98 (9 is square, 8 is neither, so the last digit must be prime):

- 989, 988: last digit isn't prime ✗
- 987: prime 7 ✓, but digit sum 24 → divisible by 3 ✗
- 986: 6 isn't prime ✗
- **985**: prime 5 ✓, digit sum 22 → not divisible by 3 ✓

**Answer: 985**

source.paper: Problem of the Week 2025-26 (from Volume 3, Set 7, Olympiad 2, 2E)

prompt:
A pile of coins sits on a table. Sarah takes half of the coins plus 4 more. Then Nick takes 2. Then Joe takes 2 more than half of what is left. Finally Selena takes 5. Four coins remain on the table.

**How many coins were on the table to start with?**

solutions.title: Work backwards
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea. Undo each step, starting from the end:

| Person (last to first) | What they did | Coins before they came |
|---|---|---|
| Selena | took 5, left 4 | $4 + 5 = 9$ |
| Joe | took half + 2, left 9 | $9 + 2 = 11$ is half, so $22$ |
| Nick | took 2, left 22 | $24$ |
| Sarah | took half + 4, left 24 | $24 + 4 = 28$ is half, so $56$ |

**Answer: 56 coins**

solutions.title: Check by working forwards
solutions.body:
Start with 56:

- Sarah takes $28 + 4 = 32$ → 24 left.
- Nick takes 2 → 22 left.
- Joe takes $11 + 2 = 13$ → 9 left.
- Selena takes 5 → **4 left** ✓

**Answer: 56 coins**

source.paper: Problem of the Week 2025-26 (from Volume 3, Set 7, Olympiad 1, 1C)

prompt:
Three friends play a series of 8 games. For each game, the winner scores 8 points, the friend in second place scores 3 points, and the friend in last place scores 0 points. At the end of 8 games, Keri's score is 20 points.

**In how many of the games did Keri finish last?**

solutions.title: Figure out how many times Keri won
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea.

- 3 or more wins would give at least 24 points — too many.
- 2 wins = 16 points, leaving 4 points, which can't come from 3-point second places. ✗
- 0 wins: 20 points all from 3s — but 20 isn't a multiple of 3. ✗
- 1 win = 8 points, leaving 12 points = 4 second places ✓
- Keri won 1 game and was second in 4 games, so she was last in $8 - 1 - 4 = 3$ games.

**Answer: 3 games**

solutions.title: Count the second places first
solutions.body:
- Keri's points come from 8s and 3s. Try numbers of second places (3 points each) and see if the rest is a multiple of 8:
  - 0 seconds: 20 left — not a multiple of 8 ✗
  - 1: 17 ✗, 2: 14 ✗, 3: 11 ✗
  - **4 seconds: 12 points, leaving 8 = one win** ✓
  - 5: 5 ✗, 6: 2 ✗
- So 1 win + 4 seconds = 5 games; the remaining $8 - 5 = 3$ games she finished last.

**Answer: 3 games**

source.paper: Problem of the Week 2025-26 (from Volume 3, Set 4, Olympiad 4, 4C)

prompt:
The tower shown is made of congruent cubes stacked on top of each other. Some of the cubes are not visible.

**How many cubes in all are used to form the tower?**

solutions.title: Count layer by layer
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea. Count visible plus hidden cubes in each layer:

| Layer | Visible + hidden | Total |
|---|---|---|
| 1 (top) | 1 + 0 | 1 |
| 2 | 2 + 1 | 3 |
| 3 | 3 + 3 | 6 |
| 4 (bottom) | 4 + 6 | 10 |

$1 + 3 + 6 + 10 = 20$ cubes.

**Answer: 20 cubes**

solutions.title: Each layer is a triangle
solutions.body:
- Looking down from above, each layer is a triangle of cubes, and each layer has one more row than the one above it.
- Top layer: 1. Next: $1 + 2 = 3$. Next: $1 + 2 + 3 = 6$. Bottom: $1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10$.
- Total: $1 + 3 + 6 + 10 = 20$.

**Answer: 20 cubes**

source.paper: Problem of the Week 2025-26 (from Volume 3, Set 13, Olympiad 2, 2C)

prompt:
Mr. Alvarez gives each of his students 4 sheets of paper and 16 sheets are left over. But if two students were absent, each of the remaining students would receive 5 sheets, with only 3 sheets left over.

**How many sheets of paper does Mr. Alvarez have?**

solutions.title: Combine the two cases
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea.

- Suppose 2 students are absent and he still gives 4 sheets each. He has the 16 leftover sheets **plus** the 8 sheets the absent students would have gotten: 24 sheets.
- Those 24 sheets give each present student 1 more sheet (making 5 each), with 3 left over. So $24 - 3 = 21$ students are present.
- Total paper: $21 \times 5 + 3 = 108$.

**Answer: 108 sheets**

solutions.title: Guess and check the class size
solutions.body:
Let the class have $s$ students. Then the paper is $4s + 16$, and also $5(s - 2) + 3$.

| Students | $4s + 16$ | $5(s-2) + 3$ |
|---|---|---|
| 20 | 96 | 93 |
| 22 | 104 | 103 |
| 23 | **108** | **108** ✓ |

**Answer: 108 sheets**

source.paper: Problem of the Week 2025-26 (from Volume 3, Set 12, Olympiad 3, 3C)

prompt:
Ali and Ben have a total of 36 CDs. After Ali gives Ben 40% of her CDs, Ben has twice as many as Ali.

**How many CDs did Ali have originally?**

solutions.title: Work backwards
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea.

- At the end, Ben has twice as many as Ali and together they have 36. So Ali has 12 and Ben has 24.
- Ali gave away 40% $= \frac{2}{5}$ of her CDs, so the 12 she kept is $\frac{3}{5}$ of what she started with.
- $\frac{1}{5}$ of her original number is $12 \div 3 = 4$, so she started with $5 \times 4 = 20$.

**Answer: 20 CDs**

solutions.title: Check possible starting numbers
solutions.body:
Ali's number must be a multiple of 5 (so 40% is a whole number). Try:

| Ali starts | Gives (40%) | Ali ends | Ben ends | Ben = 2 × Ali? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 15 | 6 | 9 | 27 | no (3×) |
| 20 | 8 | 12 | 24 | **yes** ✓ |
| 25 | 10 | 15 | 21 | no |

**Answer: 20 CDs**

prompt:
A bookseller has 15 different novels: 4 are in German, 5 are in Spanish, and 6 are in French. Emma buys two novels. They are written in two different languages.

**In how many different ways can this be done?** (Ignore the order in which she buys them.)

solutions.title: Count each pair of languages
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea.

- German + Spanish: $4 \times 5 = 20$ ways
- German + French: $4 \times 6 = 24$ ways
- Spanish + French: $5 \times 6 = 30$ ways

Total: $20 + 24 + 30 = 74$ ways.

**Answer: 74 ways**

solutions.title: All pairs minus same-language pairs
solutions.body:
- Any 2 of the 15 novels: $15 \times 14 \div 2 = 105$ pairs.
- Same-language pairs: German $4 \times 3 \div 2 = 6$, Spanish $5 \times 4 \div 2 = 10$, French $6 \times 5 \div 2 = 15$. Total 31.
- Different languages: $105 - 31 = 74$.

**Answer: 74 ways**

source.paper: Problem of the Week 2025-26 (from Volume 3, Set 16, Olympiad 4, 4C)

prompt:
A sports arena has a total capacity of 20,000 fans and ushers. One usher is required for every 30 fans.

**What is the greatest number of fans that can be in attendance?**

solutions.title: Make groups of 31
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea.

- Each group of 30 fans needs 1 usher: a group of 31 people.
- $20{,}000 \div 31 = 645$ groups with 5 people left over.
- Those 5 leftover people can't all be fans — any fans among them need an usher too. Best: 4 fans + 1 usher.
- Ushers: $645 + 1 = 646$. Fans: $20{,}000 - 646 = 19{,}354$.

**Answer: 19,354 fans**

solutions.title: Estimate, then check
solutions.body:
- About $\frac{30}{31}$ of the people can be fans: $20{,}000 \times \frac{30}{31} \approx 19{,}354.8$.
- Try 19,355 fans: they need $19{,}355 \div 30 = 645.2$, so 646 ushers. Total $19{,}355 + 646 = 20{,}001$ — too many ✗
- Try 19,354 fans: they need 646 ushers. Total $19{,}354 + 646 = 20{,}000$ ✓

**Answer: 19,354 fans**

source.paper: Problem of the Week 2025-26 (from Volume 3, Set 11, Olympiad 5, 5D)

prompt:
Starting at the same time on opposite shores of a lake, two boats cross back and forth for 35 minutes without stopping. One boat needs 5 minutes to cross the lake. The other boat needs 7 minutes.

**What is the number of times during the 35 minutes that the faster boat passes the slower boat going in the same or opposite direction?**

solutions.title: Draw a time diagram
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea.

- Draw two lines for the two shores and mark time 0 to 35 minutes along them.
- The slower boat touches alternate shores at 7, 14, 21, 28 and 35 minutes. The faster boat touches alternate shores at 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30 and 35 minutes.
- Draw each boat's zig-zag path. Every place where the two zig-zags cross is a time when the boats pass each other.
- Counting the crossings gives **7**.

**Answer: 7 times**

solutions.title: Track the meetings in order
solutions.body:
Measure the lake as 35 "steps" so the fast boat goes 7 steps a minute and the slow boat 5 steps a minute. Fast starts at shore A (step 0), slow at shore B (step 35).

- About 2.9 min: first meeting, heading toward each other.
- 8.75 min: the fast boat catches the slow boat from behind (both heading the same way).
- About 14.6 min: meet head-on.
- 17.5 min: they meet again, in the middle of the lake.
- About 20.4 min: head-on again.
- 26.25 min: fast catches up from behind again.
- About 32.1 min: last head-on meeting before 35 min (at 35 min they are on opposite shores).

That is 7 meetings.

**Answer: 7 times**

prompt:
A package weighs $P$ pounds, $P$ being a whole number. To ship this package by express costs \$1.65 for the first five pounds and 12¢ for each additional pound. The total shipping cost was \$3.45.

**How many pounds did the package weigh?**

solutions.title: Take off the first five pounds
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea.

- Total \$3.45 − \$1.65 for the first 5 pounds = \$1.80 for the extra pounds.
- $\$1.80 \div 12¢ = 180 \div 12 = 15$ extra pounds.
- Total weight: $5 + 15 = 20$ pounds.

**Answer: 20 pounds**

solutions.title: Count up
solutions.body:
- 5 pounds: \$1.65.
- Every 5 more pounds adds $5 \times 12¢ = 60¢$: 10 lb → \$2.25, 15 lb → \$2.85, 20 lb → **\$3.45** ✓

**Answer: 20 pounds**

source.paper: Problem of the Week 2025-26 (from Volume 1, Olympiad 56, #3)

prompt:
Below is a 3 by 3 by 3 cube. Not all of the cubes are visible. Suppose the entire outside of the cube is painted red, including the bottom.

**How many different 2 by 2 by 2 cubes with exactly three red faces can be found in the shown cube?**

solutions.title: Look at the corners
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea.

- A 2×2×2 cube inside the big cube has red on a face only where that face lies on the outside of the big cube.
- Every 2×2×2 cube touches exactly one corner of the 3×3×3 cube, and its outside faces are the three faces meeting at that corner.
- So **each** 2×2×2 cube has exactly three red faces — and there is one for each of the 8 corners.

**Answer: 8**

solutions.title: Count all the 2×2×2 cubes
solutions.body:
- Along each direction (left-right, front-back, up-down), a 2-wide block can start in position 1 or position 2: 2 choices.
- So there are $2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8$ different 2×2×2 cubes.
- Each one includes a corner of the big cube, so three of its faces are on the outside (red) and the other three are inside (unpainted). All 8 work.

**Answer: 8**

source.paper: Problem of the Week 2025-26 (from Volume 1, Olympiad 56, #4)

prompt:
The cold water faucet of a bathtub can fill the tub in 15 minutes. The drain, when opened, can empty the full tub in 20 minutes. Suppose the tub is empty and the faucet and drain are both opened at the same time.

**How long will it take to fill the tub?**

solutions.title: Work per minute
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea.

- Each minute the faucet fills $\frac{1}{15}$ of the tub and the drain empties $\frac{1}{20}$.
- Together: $\frac{1}{15} - \frac{1}{20} = \frac{4}{60} - \frac{3}{60} = \frac{1}{60}$ of the tub per minute.
- So the whole tub takes **60 minutes**.

**Answer: 60 minutes**

solutions.title: Pick a tub size
solutions.body:
- Pretend the tub holds 60 gallons (60 works with both 15 and 20).
- The faucet adds $60 \div 15 = 4$ gallons a minute. The drain removes $60 \div 20 = 3$ gallons a minute.
- Net gain: 1 gallon a minute → 60 minutes to fill 60 gallons.

**Answer: 60 minutes**

source.paper: Problem of the Week 2025-26 (from Volume 2, Set 15, Olympiad 5, 5A)

prompt:
A quart of milk can feed either 6 cats or 10 kittens. Suppose there are 3 quarts of milk and 15 cats.

**After all the cats are fed, how many kittens can be fed with the leftover milk?**

solutions.title: Feed all the cats first
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea.

- 1 quart feeds 6 cats, so 15 cats need $15 \div 6 = 2\frac{1}{2}$ quarts.
- Leftover: $3 - 2\frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{2}$ quart.
- 1 quart feeds 10 kittens, so $\frac{1}{2}$ quart feeds **5** kittens.

**Answer: 5 kittens**

solutions.title: Trade cats for kittens
solutions.body:
- 3 quarts could feed $3 \times 6 = 18$ cats. With 15 cats, there is milk for 3 more cats left over.
- 6 cats drink the same as 10 kittens, so 3 cats drink the same as 5 kittens.

**Answer: 5 kittens**

source.paper: Problem of the Week 2025-26 (from Volume 2, Set 6, Olympiad 3, 3A)

prompt:
Dr. Bolton was born in an interesting year. The tens digit was twice the thousands digit, the ones digit was three times the tens digit, and the hundreds digit was equal to the sum of the other three digits.

**In what year was she born?**

solutions.title: One condition at a time
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea.

- If the thousands digit were 2 or more, the tens digit would be 4 or more and the ones digit 12 or more — impossible. So the thousands digit is **1**. (She *was* born, so the year is in the past anyway.)
- Tens = $2 \times 1 = 2$ → 1 _ 2 _
- Ones = $3 \times 2 = 6$ → 1 _ 2 6
- Hundreds = $1 + 2 + 6 = 9$ → **1926**

**Answer: 1926**

solutions.title: Chain the digits
solutions.body:
Call the thousands digit $t$. Then tens = $2t$, ones = $3 \times 2t = 6t$, hundreds = $t + 2t + 6t = 9t$.

- Every digit must be 9 or less, so $9t \le 9$, which means $t = 1$.
- Digits: 1, 9, 2, 6 → 1926.

**Answer: 1926**

prompt:
At Hudson High School, the first class starts at 8:26 AM and the fourth class ends at 11:26 AM. There are 4 minutes between classes and each class is the same length.

**How many minutes are there in one class period?**

solutions.title: Subtract the passing time
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea.

class – passing – class – passing – class – passing – class

- From 8:26 to 11:26 is 3 hours = 180 minutes.
- There are only **3** passing periods between 4 classes: $3 \times 4 = 12$ minutes.
- Class time: $180 - 12 = 168$ minutes for 4 classes.
- One class: $168 \div 4 = 42$ minutes.

**Answer: 42 minutes**

solutions.title: Check a guess on the clock
solutions.body:
Try 42-minute classes:

- Class 1: 8:26–9:08, break to 9:12
- Class 2: 9:12–9:54, break to 9:58
- Class 3: 9:58–10:40, break to 10:44
- Class 4: 10:44–**11:26** ✓

**Answer: 42 minutes**

prompt:
Each of three darts lands in a numbered region of the dart board, scoring the number of points shown.

**How many different sums are possible for the three darts?**

solutions.title: Look at the differences between scores
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea.

- The smallest sum is $3 \times 2 = 6$ and the largest is $3 \times 8 = 24$.
- The scores 2, 5, 8 go up by 3 each time. So moving any dart to the next ring up adds 3 to the sum.
- That means every sum is a multiple of 3 from 6 to 24: 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21, 24.

**Answer: 7 sums**

solutions.body:
List the three scores from biggest to smallest:

| Darts | Sum |
|---|---|
| 8, 8, 8 | 24 |
| 8, 8, 5 | 21 |
| 8, 8, 2 / 8, 5, 5 | 18 |
| 8, 5, 2 / 5, 5, 5 | 15 |
| 8, 2, 2 / 5, 5, 2 | 12 |
| 5, 2, 2 | 9 |
| 2, 2, 2 | 6 |

There are 7 different sums.

**Answer: 7 sums**

source.paper: Problem of the Week 2025-26 (from Volume 2, Set 17, Olympiad 2, 2D)

prompt:
A fenced rectangular garden is 10 m wide and 20 m long. When one side is moved outward and two other sides are increased in length, the area increases by 40 sq m.

**What is the fewest number of meters of additional fencing needed to form the larger rectangular garden?**

solutions.title: Draw both possibilities
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea. There are two ways to move a side:

1. Move a **10 m side** outward. To add 40 sq m, the strip is 10 m wide, so it must be $40 \div 10 = 4$ m long. The two 20 m sides each grow by 4 m: **8 m** of new fence.
2. Move a **20 m side** outward. The strip is 20 m wide, so it must be $40 \div 20 = 2$ m deep. The two 10 m sides each grow by 2 m: **4 m** of new fence.

The fewest is 4 m.

**Answer: 4 m**

solutions.title: Use the new garden's size
solutions.body:
- The new area is $200 + 40 = 240$ sq m, and one side stays the same.
- Keep the 20 m side: the other side becomes $240 \div 20 = 12$ m (was 10). Two sides grow by 2 m each → 4 m extra.
- Keep the 10 m side: the other side becomes $240 \div 10 = 24$ m (was 20). Two sides grow by 4 m each → 8 m extra.
- The smaller amount is 4 m.

**Answer: 4 m**

prompt:
A single story house is to be built on a rectangular lot 70 feet wide by 100 feet deep. The shorter side of the lot is along the street. The house must be set back 30 feet from the street. It also must be 20 feet from the back lot line and 10 feet from each side lot line.

**What is the greatest area that the house can have, in sq ft?**

solutions.title: Draw a diagram
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea.

- Width of the house: the lot is 70 ft wide, minus 10 ft on each side: $70 - 10 - 10 = 50$ ft.
- Depth of the house: the lot is 100 ft deep, minus 30 ft in front and 20 ft in back: $100 - 30 - 20 = 50$ ft.
- Largest area: $50 \times 50 = 2500$ sq ft.

**Answer: 2500 sq ft**

solutions.title: Subtract the setback strips
solutions.body:
- Whole lot: $70 \times 100 = 7000$ sq ft.
- The house can fill the rectangle left after removing the strips. Front + back strips take 50 ft of the depth; side strips take 20 ft of the width.
- Remaining rectangle: $(70 - 20) \times (100 - 50) = 50 \times 50 = 2500$ sq ft.

**Answer: 2500 sq ft**

source.paper: Problem of the Week 2025-26 (from Volume 2, Set 10, Olympiad 2, 2C)

prompt:
Amanda, Beth, and Sarah run three races. In each race, one of them earns 5 points, one of them earns 3 points, and one of them earns 1 point. After the three races Beth has the highest point total.

**What is the smallest total score that Beth can have?**

solutions.title: Find the total points
solutions.body:
This is the official MOEMS idea.

- Each race gives out $5 + 3 + 1 = 9$ points, so 3 races give out 27 points.
- If all three tied, each would have 9. Beth has the most, so she has **more than 9**.
- Each score is the sum of three odd numbers, so it's odd. The smallest odd number above 9 is 11.
- 11 really works: Beth 5 + 5 + 1 = 11, Amanda 3 + 3 + 3 = 9, Sarah 1 + 1 + 5 = 7.

**Answer: 11 points**

solutions.title: Try small scores for Beth
solutions.body:
- Beth with 9 or less: the other two share at least 18, so one of them has at least 9 — Beth wouldn't be strictly highest.
- Beth's score is three odd numbers added, so it is odd; 10 is impossible.
- Beth with 11: the others share 16, e.g. 9 and 7. Races: (Beth, Amanda, Sarah) = (5, 3, 1), (5, 3, 1), (1, 3, 5). Totals 11, 9, 7 ✓

**Answer: 11 points**
